case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated November 15, 1993 passed by the High Court Division in Appeal from Original Order (FMA) No. 133 of 1991) and From the Judgment and Order dated January 26, 1994 passed by the High Court Division in Appeal from Original Order (FMA) No. 134 of 1991)
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: These 2 appeals, by leave, are directed against the judgment and order dated November 15, 1993 of a Division Bench of the High Court Division in First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 133 of 1991 allowing the same upon reversing the judgment and order dated February 20, 1990 of the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Chittagong, in Miscellaneous Case No. 315 of 1988 allowing the same and the judgment and order dated January 26, 1994 of a Division Bench of the High Court Division in First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 134 of 1991 allowing the same upon reversing the judgment and order dated February 20, 1990 of the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Chittagong, in Miscellaneous Case No. 314 of 1988 allowing the same, respectively.

2. Pre-emption was sought under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in respect of 381/2 decimals of land in each of the Miscellaneous cases. The land sought to be pre-empted was transferred by two kabalas dated June 25, 1988.

3. The land originally belonged to Khan Bahadur Aman Ali and the RS Khatian No. 791 /1 was prepared in his name. The pre-emptor by different kabalas of the years 1981 and 1982 in total purchased 1.80 acre of land from the heirs of Khan Bahadur Aman Ali and also from the co-sharer tenant of the RS Khatian No. 791/1.

4. The Miscellaneous Cases were filed stating, inter alia, that by the 2 separate kabalas of June 25, 1988 the heirs of Khan Bahadur Aman Ali without serving notice to the co-sharers have sold the land of the aforesaid R S Khatian to the pre-emptees and fact of purchase was first disclosed to the pre-emptor's husband on July 10, 1988 and having had the information of transfer the pre-emptor obtained certified copies of the kabalas on July 18 and 19, 1988 and thereupon requested the pre-emptees to re-transfer the land so purchased by them to her on accepting price as mentioned in the kabalas as well as the compensation as provide by the law, but they denied finally on July 30, 1988. The pre-emptees are strangers in the holding and also not co-sharers of the land so transferred.

5. The pre-emptor claimed pre-emption as of being the co-sharer of the ejmali land of the holding i.e. RS Khatian No. 791/1, and that the land sought to be pre-empted is contiguous to the land whereof he is a co-sharer.

6. The prayer for pre-emption was opposed by filing written objections stating, amongst others, that the prayer for pre-emption sought under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is not maintainable since the land being within the Chittagong Municipality is non-agricultural land, that the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer of the holding since the jama has been separated by the pre-emptor as well as by the pre-emptees, that pre-emptor is not a contiguous land holder in respect of the land sought to be pre-empted since there is a pathway separating the land sought to be pre-empted from the land owned by the pre-emptor, that the land sought to be pre-empted being non-agricultural land claim of pre-emption on the claim of being contiguous land owner is not available to the pre-emptor.

7. The trial Court by separate judgments of the same date allowed the Miscellaneous Cases upon holding that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer of the holding, that the Miscellaneous Case Nos.1134 of 1986-87 and 561 of 1986-87, on the basis whereof jama is claimed to have been separated by the pre-emptor, were not filed by him and notices of the said Miscellaneous Cases were not served on the co-sharers of the jama and, as such, there was no separation of jama in the eye of law and consequently, the pre-emptor remained co-sharer of the jama. The trial Court also held that order in Mutation Case No. 550 of 1988-89 by which pre-emptees are said to have separated the jama was obtained during pendency of the Miscellaneous Cases and no notice of the said Miscellaneous Case was served on the co-sharers of the holding. The trial Court further held that although the land is within the municipal area, but the said land being agricultural land there no bar for the pre-emptor to have the relief sought in the Miscellaneous Cases and that no evidence was brought on record by the pre-emptees to establish that brick built 3' width 'ail' is a municipal road and that there was no amicable partition of ejmali land and the land of the jama was not partitioned by the decree of the Court. The trial Court also found that the Miscellaneous Cases were not bad for defect of parties or barred by limitation. Finally, the trial Court allowed Miscellaneous Cases upon placing reliance on the decision in the case reported in 27 DLR (AD) 114 wherein it has been observed that merely for wrong mentioning of the provision of law in the cause title of the petition seeking pre-emption, the petitioner should not be denied the relief sought since by converting the application so filed under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act to an application under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act same could be given as it was proved that the pre-emptor is entitled to seek pre-emption and to get the relief prayed for in the Miscellaneous Case and it was not necessary to apply for amendment for a change of description in the cause title.

8. The pre-emptees as against the judgment and order of the trial Court took appeals as mentioned hereinbefore.

9. The appeal, i.e.- Miscellaneous Appeal No. 133 of 1991, filed against the judgment and order passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 315 of 1988 was allowed by the High Court Division by the judgment and order dated November 15, 1993 upon observing, amongst others, that the Miscellaneous Cases for separation of jama were not filed by the pre-emptor and that the notices of the Miscellaneous Cases were not served on the co-sharers and, as such, it cannot be found for certainty that the jama was separated, that pre-emptor was competent to seek preemption as co-sharer of the jama but since she has sought pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in respect of the land which is non-agricultural land being within the Chittagong Municipality the Miscellaneous case was not maintainable and that no application seeking amendment was filed for converting to a case under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act. The High Court Division also rejected the prayer for pre-emption on the ground of contiguity upon observing that "As there is a pathway in between the lands it cannot be found that the petitioner has land contiguous to the case land,"

10. The other Appeal i.e. Miscellaneous Appeal No. 134 of 1991, filed against the judgment and order passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 314 of 1988 was also allowed by the High Court Division on January 26, 1994 on the finding that the 'ail' or pathway separates the case land from the land of the pre-emptor and, as such, pre-emptor is not a contiguous land owner of the case land and consequently, his claim of pre-emption on that score is not available to him and the land being within the Chittagong Municipality is not an agricultural land and, as such, prayer for pre-emption made by filing application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was not available and the Miscellaneous case filed seeking pre-emption was not maintainable since there was separation of jama and that the separation so made was acted upon by payment of rent, and the 'same was tried to be established by the pre-emptees showing payment of rent of the separated jama and that "Though there is nothing on record to show at whose instance the Mutation Case was started the fact remains that the order of separation of the jama has been passed and the Dakhilas Exhibit H proved the payment of rent" and that genuineness of that Exhibit H was not challenged by the pre-emptor and that though notices of the Mutation case was not served on the co-sharers but the fact remains that rent was paid in respect of the jama so separated and "When the order has been acted upon on payment of rent the plea that no notice has been served on the respondent for separation of the jama cannot be sustained. Further, it appears that immediately after the knowing of the separation of the jama no appeal has been preferred against the order passed by the Revenue Officer indicating also that the separation of the jama has been accepted. The mere fact that notice of the mutation proceeding has not been served on the respondent cannot defeat the final order passed by the Revenue Officer when on the basis of that a separate Khatian was opened and rents paid by the petitioner-respondent. The non-filing of the petition for mutation and non-production of the service return of the notice cannot be a ground to ignore the final order of mutation due to the fact that the same has been acted upon as before" and that as the jama was separated the pre-emptor ceased to be a co-sharer of the holding for getting a pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act.

11. It may be mentioned in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 314 of 1991 the learned Advocate of the pre-emptor-respondent filed an application seeking conversion of the petition filed under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act to a petition under section 24 of the Non Agricultural and Tenancy Act, but the same was rejected on the finding that the application so filed was neither verified, nor supported by affidavit and, as such, cannot be considered a petition for amendment of plaint of Miscellaneous case.

12. Leave was granted to consider the Submissions that the High Court. Division committed an error of law in holding that pre-emption could not be allowed under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act without amendment of the application for pre-emption filed tinder section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act pursuant to a proper application by the pre-emptors to that end and that the findings about the separation of the holding concerned in both the pre-emption cases being contradictory to each other as given in First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 133 of 1991 and First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 134 of 1991 requires reconsideration and re-conciliation.

13. The land sought to be pre-empted is undisputedly within the Chittagong Municipality and, as such, the pre-emptor (appellant in both the appeals) was required to seek preemption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act, but petition seeking pre-emption was filed under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, as it appears since the land sought to be pre-empted was described in the kabalas as "কৃষি নাল জমি ". Be that as it may, it appears from the judgment of the High Court Division that the said Division rejected the prayer for pre-emption, amongst others, that the petition seeking preemption was filed under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and that no proper application seeking amendment to convert the petition so filed to a petition under section 24 of the Non Agricultural and Tenancy Act was filed.

14. The learned Counsel for the appellant, in both the appeals, has submitted that mis-quoting or non-quoting of the provision of law in the cause title of the plaint, herein in the petition for pre-emption, cannot be a ground for refusing the relief sought for if in the background of the facts established the relief so sought for is available, nor the Court is incompetent to allow the relief sought for, or, in other words, the Court should not refuse the relief sought for merely because the provision of law under which the relief so sought for has not been correctly put in the cause title of the plaint. In support of the aforesaid submission, the learned Counsel has referred us to the case of Jadav Chandra Mali vs Abdul Khaleque and others reported in 27 DLR (AD) 114 wherein it has been observed if the relief claimed is available under some other law other than the law mentioning which relief has been sought before the Court, then the Court is "bound to apply the same notwithstanding the misdescription of the cause title.”

15. The learned Counsel for the pre-emptee-respondent has submitted that in the absence of duly verified application seeking amendment the Court is quite competent, as in the instant cases, to refuse the relief sought for. To substantiate the said submission the learned Counsel has referred to Rule 17(2) and Rule 19 of the Civil Rules and Orders.

16. True pleadings as well as petitions of all kinds requiring judicial investigation or determination require to be verified in the manner as provided in Order VI rule 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure, but, in our view, in a fit case while in the background of the material(s) brought on record relief sought for requires to be allowed or given, in that situation on mere technicality, like mis-quoting or non-quoting of the provision of law in the cause title of the pleading or petition, or that for the absence of formal petition conforming to requirement of law the relief sought for instead of refusing the same is to be given to advance the cause of justice and to ameliorate the condition of aggrieved for which the Court exists.

17. It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division, in both the appeals, that the said Division found that it was not established that the pre-emptor or pre-emptees filed the application seeking separation of the jama and that it was not established that notices of the Miscellaneous Cases started for separating the jama were served upon the co-sharers of the holding and thereupon in First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 133 of 1991 the High Court Division held that there was no separation of jama, but in First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 134 of 1991 the said Division in spite of holding that it was not established that the petition seeking separation of the jama was filed either by the pre-emptor or pre-emptees and that notices were served on the co-sharers of the holding but still then held that it cannot be said that there was no separation of holding since the fact of separation of the holding was acted upon by paying rent. It may be mentioned payment of rent was sought to be established from the side of the pre-emptees.

18. In the afore state of the matter it was urged at the time of obtaining leave that the contrary findings of the High Court Division as to separation of jama needs reconsideration and re-conciliation.

19. The learned Counsel for the appellant upon referring to the case of Md Jabed Ali and others vs Rakhal Chandra Mondal and others reported in 33 DLR (AD) 309 has submitted that in view of the provision in section 117(1)(c) an order of the Revenue Officer separating holding would be valid only when the same is made in conformity with the provision of the said section of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act i.e. there must be an application from one or more co-sharer tenants seeking separation of holding and that an order of separation of holding shall have to be made upon serving reasonable notice "to the parties concerned to appear and be heard in the matter".

20. The learned Counsel submits that the High Court Division found that it was established before the Court that application in Miscellaneous Case No. 1134 of 1986-87 or Miscellaneous Case No. 561 of 1986-87 was not filed by the pre-emptor and that notices of the said Miscellaneous Cases were not served on the co-sharers of the holding and that it was also not established that Mutation Case No. 550 of 1988-89 was filed by the pre-emptees and that notice of the same was not served on the pre-emptor and pre-emptee as well as on the other co-sharers of the holding and thus as there was no separation of holding the High Court Division was in error in reversing the judgment and order of the trial Court allowing pre-emption on the finding that pre-emptor is a co-sharer. It may be mentioned in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 133 of 1991 High Court Division reversed judgment of the trial Court on the sole ground that the land sought to be pre-empted is within the municipality and consequently, being nonagricultural land pre-emption application filed under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was not maintainable.

21. The learned Counsel for the pre-emptee-respondents has submitted that non-serving of notice in separating the jama was a mere irregularity and that as the pre-emptor did not file any appeal as against the order of the Revenge Officer he was precluded from taking exception to the order so passed by the competent Revenue Officer and that the Court is not competent to ignore the order so passed by the Revenue Officer on the ground of mere irregularity. In support of the aforesaid contention, the learned Counsel has referred to the case reported in 33 DLR (AD) 309 wherein it has been observed "If any of the tenants is aggrieved by the order, he can take recourse to appeal as provided in this section itself. In the absence of such an appeal the order becomes final and binding upon all the co-sharer tenants. When such a valid order under section 117 is on record, and the order has been given effect, the Civil Court is not competent to ignore the order on the ground of finding some irregularity in the same as a Court of appeal, while dealing with the application under section 96 of the Act for pre-emption".

22. The observations as quoted above can hardly be disputed, but the fact is that there must be an order separating the jama by a competent Revenue Officer in conformity with the statutory requirements is are in section 117(1)(c) of the SAT Act and the first proviso thereto. In the instant case both from the judgment of the High Court Division as well as of the trial Court it in seen that it was not established by the pre-emptees that an order in conformity with the provision of section 117(1)(c) of the SAT Act and the first proviso thereto was made. In that view of the matter, the contention of the learned Counsel for the pre-emptee-respondents since the pre-emptor did not take appeal as against the order of the Revenue Officer the order has become final and binding on the pre-emptor is not legally well founded. An order of a competent Revenue Officer separating the jama in strict compliance of the provision of section 117 (1)(c) of the SAT Act if not appealed only then it becomes final and binding upon all the co-sharers of the holding and in other case(B) it is not.

23. The learned Counsel for the respondent in support of his contention that pre-emptor was not entitled to the relief sought for since there was separation of the jama and consequent thereupon new khatians were opened and rent was paid and thus fact of separation of jama being a concluded one or, in other words, there was ceasing of co-sharership the High Court Division was quite legal in reversing the judgment of the trial Court allowing preemption has referred to the case of Md Khairullah Bhuiyan vs. Haji Nurul Alam Chowdhury reported in 35 DLR (AD) 338 wherein it has been observed "The term 'separation' is not a legal term like amalgamation" or 'subdivision’; it is not used in section 116 or 117, but nevertheless, it denotes, in general sense, separation of a share from a joint tenancy, and, as such, 'separation' necessarily means subdivision of a joint tenancy and falls under, and is governed by clause (c) of section 117. Effect of separation of a share from the joint holding falls upon all Co-sharers who, after separation, cease to be co-sharers of the original holding and the case of Fatema Bibi vs Sree Manik Lal Somaddar reported in 50 DLR (AD) 97 and also has referred to the case of SM Basiruddin vs Zahurul Islam Chowdhury and another reported in 35 DLR (AD) 230 wherein this Division noticed a Full Bench of the Dhaka High Court had held by majority decision that the two terms that 'nonagricultural land' and 'holding' are synonymous carrying the same meaning, but this Division held 'nonagricultural land' used in section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act is not synonymous with the word 'holding' as used in SAT Act. The decision in the case reported in 50 DLR (AD) 97 in the background of the facts and circumstances as well as point came up consideration is an authority for the case therein decided. We have already found that there was no legal separation of jama or holding as per provision of section 117(c) and the first proviso thereto and, as such, there was no ceasing of co-sharership either of the holding or land.

24. In reply to the aforesaid contention, the learned Counsel for the appellant has submitted that pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act is available to one or more co-sharer tenants of nonagricultural land in case of transfer of a portion or share of the non-agricultural land. It can hardly be disputed that pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act is available to one or more co-sharer tenants of non-agricultural land when a portion or share of the non-agricultural land is transferred to a stranger, or, in other words, who is not a co-sharer of the land so transferred. The submission so made in the background of the language of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act is of merit since the provision of said section of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act is explicit to the extent that for raising claim of pre-emption under the said provision the pre-emptor shall have to be co-sharer of the land transferred.

25. The learned Counsel for the pre-emptee-respondents submitted that the High Court Division was quite correct in holding that pre-emptor was not a contiguous land holder to the land sought to be pre-empted since the land of which the pre-emptor claimed to be a co-sharer is separated by an 'ail' or pathway. It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division and the trial Court that it was not established, in fact, the pathway, as claimed by the pre-emptees, that said to have separated the pre-emptor's land from the land sought to be pre-empted was a municipal road or a recorded path, rather it is seen that the claimed 3' width brick built pathway or 'ail' is for the use of the owners of the land of the holding in question. It is the assertion of the preemptor that there is an 'ail' of 3' width in between his land and the land sought to be pre-empted and to dislodge the case of the pre-emptor no material was placed on the record. Since it has not been established that the claimed pathway is of the Municipality or is a recorded path we are, of the view the High Court Division was in error in holding that pre-emptor was not a contiguous land holder to the land sought to pre-empted. It may be mentioned that The land of RS Khatian No. 791/1 is the 'ejmali' land of the recorded tenants and the same was never partitioned amongst the co-sharers either by the decree of the Court or by any other mode of partition.

26. The learned Counsel for the pre-emptee-respondents also submitted since sufficient time had passed from the time of filing the Miscellaneous Cases upon mentioning wrong provision of law and by such passage of time right has accrued to the pre-emptees, as such, at this stage of the matter upon resorting to the provision of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act relief sought by way of pre-emption will not be an equitable and justifiable one since in case of allowing the pre-emption the pre-emptees will be deprived of their vested right and in support of the aforesaid submission has referred to the case of Abdur Rabban vs Aminul Hoque Sowdagar and another reported in 43 DLR (AD) 19 wherein it has been observed with the passage of time, question of limitation and accrual of vested rights step in and the High Court Division correctly rejected the application for amendment of the plaint. It may be observed the aforesaid observation has been made in the background of the facts and circumstances of the said case and the facts and circumstances which were present in the aforesaid case are absent in the instant case since relief in the light of the provision of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act was very much available to the pre-emptor from the very date of filing of the petition seeking pre-emption. The learned Counsel has also referred to the case of Ahmed Hossain and others vs. Basharat Ali and others reported in 32 DLR (AD) 54 wherein it has been observed "A citizen's right to deal with his property freely, in view of the special statutory provision, bears a clog, that is, subject to right of pre-emption. The statutory provision providing such a right curtailing owner's right to deal with property must be construed very strictly". It is true that in considering the prayer for pre-emption Court is to construe strictly the provision of law as to right of pre-emption. In the instant case from the material on record it is clearly seen that pre-emptor is entitled to the relief sought, but the same has been dis-allowed by the High Court Division on mere technicality in that in the application seeking pre-emption provision of law which was mentioned was not the one which ought to have been mentioned as well as upon contradictory finding as to separation of holding. We have already observed that in a situation of the first category if the Court is satisfied that the relief sought is available then because of mis-description of law in the cause title the relief should not be denied, rather Court is required to grant the relief. The second category is not legally sustainable.

<u>27. In the background of the discussion made hereinabove we are of the view that the High Court Division was in error in holding that the pre-emptor was not a co-sharer of the land sought to be pre-empted upon an erroneous view that there was separation of Jama, though in fact in the eye of law there was no separation of Jama which the High Court Division in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 133 of 1991 itself found. Moreover, the application so filed seeking pre-emption was quite maintainable since the same was filed within the time prescribed by law and that there was deposit of the amount mentioned in the kabala as well as the statutory compensation or, in Other words, deposit that was made in seeking pre-emption was not short of the amount that was required to be deposited for the purpose of maintainability of the pre-emption petition and the same was not bad for defect of parties. The application for preemption was quite in form except mis-description or misquoting of the provision of law in the cause title or, in other words, non-inserting of the correct provision of law under which relief was sought. In our view, the aforesaid state of the matter does not dis-entitle a person of the relief if the Court finds that he is entitled to the relief sought and, in such a situation, the Court is required to grant the relief sought for. In the instant Miscellaneous Cases similar thing having had happened, the Court ought to have granted the relief prayed for.</u>

28. In the background of the discussions made hereinbefore, we find merit in the appeals.

Accordingly, the appeals are allowed. There is no order as to costs.

End.
